body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Nurse-driven catheter removal protocols and catheter utilisation: a multi-hospital interrupted time series","authors":"Okoro-Lindahl B, Castellanos-Pike R, Mensah-Vogel T","year":2020,"venue":"Journal of Hospital Infection Prevention","doi":"10.5555/jhip.2020.0418","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across 9 hospitals, a nurse-driven removal protocol with daily catheter review was introduced in a staggered sequence over 18 months. Catheter utilisation fell from 21 to 14 catheter days per 100 patient days, and segmented regression showed a level change at introduction in 7 of 9 hospitals. The infection rate per 1,000 catheter days did not change clearly (2.1 before and 1.9 after), and the number of infections was too small to estimate an effect with precision. Reinsertion within 48 hours of removal followed 4 percent of removals, similar before and after. Hospitals with a named ward champion sustained the change for longer."},{"title":"Value stream mapping of the urinary catheter pathway from emergency department to ward","authors":"Varga-Holm D, Achebe-Nilsen F","year":2018,"venue":"Lean Methods in Hospital Care","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In one hospital, a team mapped the catheter pathway from insertion in the emergency department to removal on the ward, timing each step for 40 patients. Catheters inserted in the emergency department had no documented indication in 45 percent of cases, and the median wait between the first day a catheter was no longer needed and its removal was 2.5 days. Most of the wait arose at handoffs between teams, where no one owned the removal decision. After standard work and a daily huddle check, the median wait fell to 1 day in a second mapping of 40 patients. The study had no comparison group."},{"title":"Interventions to reduce catheter-associated urinary tract infection: a systematic review of controlled and time-series studies","authors":"Rahman-Keller S, Oduya-Brandt L, Petrakis-Hughes M, Sato-Obi N","year":2022,"venue":"Infection Control Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/icer.2022.0203","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included 31 studies of reminders, stop orders, nurse-driven removal and bundles. Catheter use fell in most studies, with a median relative reduction of 32 percent. Only 8 studies reported infection rates with enough events to estimate change, and their pooled rate ratio was 0.69 (95 percent CI 0.52 to 0.91), with high heterogeneity. Most studies were uncontrolled before-and-after designs at high risk of bias. Studies using interrupted time series with at least eight points before and after were less likely to report large effects."},{"title":"Measuring catheter days when electronic flowsheets are incomplete: agreement between point prevalence counts and daily records","authors":"Mbeki-Sorensen A, Laurent-Adeyemi K","year":2024,"venue":"Surveillance Methods Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"On 14 wards we compared catheter days from electronic flowsheets with estimates from twice-weekly point prevalence counts. Estimates from the counts agreed with the flowsheet within 8 percent over a month, but weekly estimates varied more, and short catheterisations under two days were missed by the counts. Wards using paper records could produce monthly utilisation from the counts with about 3 hours of staff time a month. The authors advise against mixing the two sources within one ward's time series, because a switch of source can look like a change in practice."},{"title":"Staggered rollout of improvement work across hospitals: designing for inference with multiple baselines","authors":"Lindgren-Oyelowo E, Tanaka-Ferreira J, Brennan-Quist H","year":2016,"venue":"Improvement Science Methods","doi":"10.5555/ism.2016.0031","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We describe how to plan improvement work that starts at different times in different hospitals so that each hospital acts as a control for the others while it waits. With four sites and three-month intervals, each site contributes a different baseline length, and a segmented regression with site-specific levels can separate the change at each start from secular trends. Simulations with 12 monthly points before the first start showed that staggered starts detected a 25 percent level change with 80 percent power where simultaneous starts reached 55 percent. Autocorrelation and seasonal infection patterns must be modelled explicitly."},{"title":"Catheter reinsertion after nurse-driven removal: a balancing measure","authors":"Dubois-Mwangi C, Haddad-Strand O","year":2021,"venue":"Continence and Urology Nursing","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across 6 wards, 1,240 catheter removals under a nurse-driven protocol were followed for 72 hours. Reinsertion occurred after 5.2 percent of removals, most often for urinary retention in men over 75 after surgery. A bladder scan before any reinsertion reduced unnecessary reinsertions over the following year. The authors recommend reporting reinsertion within 72 hours as a balancing measure with any removal protocol, and describing retention episodes separately so that a rise in reinsertions is not hidden inside falling catheter days."},{"title":"Why catheters stay: ward nurses on removal decisions","authors":"Nakashima-Ortiz P, Adeleke-Svensson M, Reid-Castaneda A","year":2019,"venue":"Qualitative Nursing Practice","doi":"10.5555/qnp.2019.0117","providerType":"qualitative study","abstract":"We talked with 28 ward nurses in three hospitals about decisions to remove urinary catheters. Nurses described uncertainty about whether they were allowed to remove a catheter without a physician order, fear of reinsertion if the patient could not void, and handoffs where the reason for the catheter was lost. Several described catheters left in to manage incontinence or falls risk at night. Nurses on wards with a written removal protocol described fewer delays and more confidence in raising removal at the morning huddle."}]}
